newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's top central banker sees stronger dollar.
newsitem.headline: Canada's top central banker sees stronger dollar.

text.p: Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen told a conference of the world's top currency traders on Friday that prospects were good for a stronger Canadian dollar.
"For cyclical as well as for more fundamental reasons, the prospects are good for a stronger Canadian currency," Thiessen said in a speech at the World Forex Conference in Toronto.
The head of Canada's central bank said the country's improved fiscal position, low inflation and strengthening economy all pointed to an appreciation in the currency.
The Canadian dollar strengthened after Thiessen's comments, rising past C$1.38 (72.46 U.S. cents) from the morning's open of C$1.3819 (72.36 U.S. cents).

"Inflation in Canada is stable, at its lowest level in decades. And it has been somewhat below that in the United States since 1992. This implies a potential appreciation in the Canadian dollar vis-a-vis the U.S. dollar over time, if the inflation differential persists," Thiessen said.
He said other factors aiding the dollar included deficit reduction by Canadian governments, improved competitiveness by Canadian companies and a likely pickup in primary commodity prices.

"In light of all this, it is not surpising that several analysts, as well as the Bank of Canada, expect a stronger Canadian dollar in the future and think that the currency is currently undervalued relative to its longer term fundamentals," Thiessen said.
Thiessen said Canada's policy of keeping monetary conditions relatively stimulative was "temporarily" appropriate because the economy was operating below capacity and inflation remained subdued.
But he said prospects were good for robust expansion in 1997 and 1998, which should absorb the slack in the economy without causing inflation.
As the excess capacity was taken up, the central bank would shift to a less accommodative monetary policy, he said.
"As the slack is absorbed, the Bank will need to pursue less stimulative monetary conditions, consistent with a durable, low-inflation economic expansion, said Thiessen.
Speaking to reporters after the speech, Thiessen declined to comment on Canada's federal election next Monday.

"Central bankers should be snug in their offices on the eve of an election and not out talking to the press," said Thiessen. "This is a time for Canadians to listen to politicians, not central bankers."
